facts.statement: Sourcify holds 43,781,389 verified contracts.
facts.scope: distinct verified contracts across all chains, from Sourcify's own stats dashboard

facts.statement: 29.1% of verified contracts are exact matches and 70.9% are partial matches (12,737,278 and 31,044,111).
facts.scope: share of the 43.78M verified contracts

facts.statement: An exact match means the compiler-embedded metadata hash in the bytecode also matches, proving the source is byte-for-byte what was deployed, down to comments and whitespace. A partial match means the compiled bytecode matches on chain but the metadata hash does not: behaviour is identical, but comments, variable names or file paths may differ.
facts.scope: Sourcify verification semantics

facts.statement: Sourcify grew roughly 4x in eight months: 11M verified contracts at the end of 2025, 38.5M by 1 July 2026, 43.78M today.
facts.scope: Sourcify's own published figures at three dates; we did NOT establish the cause

facts.statement: Sourcify absorbs about 34,639 new verifications per day on a 7-day average, and 37,545 on a 30-day average, excluding bulk imports.
facts.scope: organic steady state; trailing windows that span July are inflated by a bulk import

facts.statement: One verification is not one row: it lands about 10.4 rows across the ten tables and adds about 25.5 KiB to the database. So ~34k verifications/day is roughly 355k rows/day and ~850 MB/day.
facts.scope: corpus average (total export rows / verified_contracts rows); the byte figure is measured from three database-size readings 11 days apart

source.label: derived from Parquet footers + export stats.json

facts.statement: Only 0.13 rows per verification land in compiled_contracts and 0.14 in sources, so roughly 87% of verifications add no new compilation and no new source file at all: the contract is a copy of something already stored.
facts.value: ~87% of verifications add no new compilation
facts.scope: corpus average; this is why blob storage scales with 5.7M compilations rather than 43.8M contracts

facts.statement: Sourcify's live Postgres database is 949.6 GB by pg_database_size, of which the ten exported tables are 692.9 GB (73.0%).
facts.scope: whole database on disk including indexes, TOAST, catalogs and free space

facts.statement: 256.7 GB (27.0%) of the database is physical footprint not explained by the ten exported relations. It could be other tables, materialized views, system catalogs or bloat -- we cannot label it without a relation inventory from Sourcify.
facts.scope: pg_database_size minus the sum of pg_total_relation_size for the ten exported tables; a residual, not a category

facts.statement: The public Parquet export is 170.4 GB across 2,687 files, zstd compressed, refreshed daily. That is 4.07x smaller than the ten exported tables and 7.45x smaller than the raw uncompressed content.
facts.scope: the v2 export at storage.googleapis.com/sourcify-production-parquet-export/v2

facts.statement: The v2 Parquet export is append-only: a full file is never rewritten, so updated rows are appended and the old version stays. sourcify_matches holds 74,196,213 rows in the export against 42,733,948 measured live, about 31.5M superseded versions or 42.4% of the export. It therefore cannot be replayed as a backfill without deduplicating by primary key.
facts.unit: % of the export that is superseded rows
facts.scope: sourcify_matches only; compiled_contracts shows the same pattern at 9.7%

facts.statement: Sourcify's database grows about 24.7 GiB per month organically (26.5 GB), measured from three pg_database_size readings across 11 days.
facts.scope: organic steady state. The widely quoted 189 GiB/month figure from their July cost issue is 7.7x higher because it was measured across a window containing a bulk import

facts.statement: On 17 July 2026 Sourcify added 2,774,661 verified contracts in a single day, which their own cost issue attributes to a similarity-import job.
facts.scope: the largest single-day jump in the recent series; bulk imports are a different regime from organic writes

facts.statement: Sourcify currently supports 267 chains out of 420 configured, and 377 chains have at least one verified contract.
facts.scope: three different metrics that must not be mixed: supported=true on the live /chains endpoint (267), total entries in /chains (420), chains appearing in the stats dataset (377)

facts.statement: Sourcify's own posts give two conflicting scopes for 15M requests/day: the Dec 2025 recap says over 15M across ALL Sourcify APIs with 4byte alone above 7M, while the May 2026 post on retiring API v1 says v2 is 'already serving 15M+ requests/day', which reads as the contract API on its own.
facts.scope: unresolved -- the difference is roughly a factor of two on any capacity target. This is question 6 to Kaan.

facts.statement: The 4byte signature service holds 9,920,797 signatures in 0.84 GB across 9.9M rows -- the smallest, most self-contained table, and it carries a large share of Sourcify's traffic. Their public /stats counter reports 9,340,765 but its own refreshed_at is 2026-07-06, so it is six weeks stale.
facts.scope: exact count from Parquet footers today; their published counter is stale

facts.statement: Sourcify's production database sends about 13.6 TB per month to its clients. Inside Google Cloud that costs zero; externally it would be roughly 1,400 USD per month, more than their entire database bill.
facts.scope: measured by Sourcify from Cloud Monitoring; an earlier figure of 15.9 TB was revised down after Kaan pushed back

facts.statement: Sourcify's entire Cloud SQL fleet costs about 1,003 USD per month across both projects, the production database 373 USD, analytics about 42 USD, and the Parquet export sits in GCS at 242 GiB for about 5 USD.
facts.scope: their July 2026 cost review; note these figures came from an AI analysis of their infra that Sourcify posted, and one number in it was later revised

facts.statement: Sourcify's Cloud CDN is switched off while 88.6% of successful GETs are repeat URLs, costing roughly 700 USD per month in uncached internet egress. Turning it on is the cheapest optimisation available to them, and any serving proposal has to acknowledge that.
facts.unit: % of successful GETs that are repeat URLs
facts.scope: measured by Sourcify while investigating egress

facts.statement: Sourcify already evaluated moving their database in July 2026 and concluded 'don't migrate'. Crucially that review compared conventional hosted Postgres providers -- Neon, Supabase, Crunchy, Aiven, Hetzner, Scaleway -- and never evaluated Arkiv. Kaan closed it saying 'it seems still too expensive to me... can be opened later'.
facts.scope: hosted Postgres alternatives only; nothing was decided about Arkiv

facts.statement: Sourcify's open issue #2924 reports that compiler metadata is stored per deployment rather than per compilation, averaging 8.5 copies. sourcify_matches is 182 GB of which 163 GB (90%) is that metadata; normalising would free about 139 GB. They cannot fix it because the shared Verifier Alliance schema has no slot for it. Our own column measurement independently confirms it: sourcify_matches.metadata is 600.3 GB of raw bytes, 99.6% of that table.
facts.scope: their estimate; our independent measurement of the metadata column agrees on the shape

facts.statement: The schema is the Verifier Alliance base shared with Blockscout and Routescan (code, contracts, contract_deployments, compiled_contracts, compiled_contracts_sources, sources, verified_contracts) plus three Sourcify tables (sourcify_matches, signatures, compiled_contracts_signatures). Those ten are what gets exported. verification_jobs, verification_jobs_ephemeral, a signature-stats materialized view and migration bookkeeping are never exported; session and sourcify_sync were dropped in March and July 2026.
facts.scope: table inventory taken from services/database/migrations in the repo

facts.statement: Sourcify's 75-byte bytecode similarity search is served by a Postgres expression index on code -- substring(code FROM 1 FOR 75) -- not a separate table. The naive implementation walked 142k rows and took 36 seconds in production before they indexed it.
facts.scope: migration 20251101120000_add_code_first_75_index

facts.statement: The main read path is GET /v2/contract/{chainId}/{address} with field selection (?fields= or ?omit=, dot-notation for nested fields). It also resolves proxies at request time, which is computed rather than stored. Other routes: /v2/contract/all-chains/{address}, a paginated /v2/contracts/{chainId} with cursor afterMatchId and limit up to 200, and POST /v2/verify/similarity/{chainId}/{address}.
facts.scope: Sourcify API v2; v1 was permanently retired on 2026-07-07

facts.statement: On our Cheesecake devnet we measured 107 entities/second sustained with 300 concurrent wallets over 30 minutes, with zero failed writes among included transactions. That figure is incomplete on its own: a large share of submissions were turned away under queue pressure, so attempted, admitted and included throughput must be reported separately.
facts.scope: PROVISIONAL. Devnet under construction, small synthetic entities, not a multi-day Sourcify-shaped workload. Do not quote to Sourcify as a capability commitment.

facts.statement: An Arkiv transaction is capped at 128 KB, which worked out to 226 entities per transaction in our devnet test. There is no documented PER-ENTITY payload ceiling, and Sourcify's heaviest metadata blocks average about 186 KB -- past a whole transaction on their own.
facts.scope: PROVISIONAL, measured on a devnet under construction. The per-entity limit is an open question for Arkiv engineering.

facts.statement: Arkiv's typed query language supports equality, ranges, AND/OR/NOT, prefix matching (STARTSWITH), field projection, cursor pagination and historical reads at a block. It does NOT have joins, aggregations, GROUP BY, server-side ORDER BY, or an inequality operator. All of this should be treated as 'exposed in an SDK' rather than 'benchmarked at scale' until engineering confirms which is which.
facts.scope: PROVISIONAL. Taken from an internal feature matrix, not from a benchmark.

facts.statement: The proposed mapping is not a row-for-row copy: Arkiv has no joins, so a faithful copy would need multiple round trips per lookup. Instead, one denormalised head entity per verified contract keyed by chainId:address, carrying the indexed attributes people filter on (chain, address, match type, compiler, version, language, contract name, code hashes, verified timestamp) plus hash references to the heavy artifacts. At ~44M head entities of ~600-800 bytes that is roughly 30 GB of entity payload; the remaining ~1,216 GB stays content-addressed exactly as Sourcify already stores it.
facts.scope: OUR PROPOSAL, not a measurement and not agreed with Sourcify

facts.statement: We do not know Sourcify's route-level read workload: the request mix per endpoint, peak requests per second, p95/p99 latency, or cache-hit ratio. A dataset snapshot is an inventory, not a workload, and none of this is in the public export.
facts.scope: Only Sourcify can answer. Unit of the answer: requests/day per route, peak RPS, p95/p99 ms, cache-hit %. An existing dashboard screenshot would do.

facts.statement: We have no benchmark of Arkiv's concurrent read capacity. The public endpoint's 50 requests/hour/IP is a gateway quota, which is policy rather than a measurement of the read engine, and our latency samples were periodic single reads rather than load. Any claim about serving Sourcify's traffic is unsupported until this is measured.
facts.scope: Arkiv engineering owns this. Unit of the answer: sustained requests/second at a given entity count and p99 latency under concurrent load.

facts.statement: It is not yet decided whether Sourcify would query a public Arkiv endpoint or run their own Arkiv node or indexer and read locally. This changes the proposal fundamentally: a self-hosted read replica sidesteps the gateway quota entirely and speaks directly to their egress problem.
facts.scope: Arkiv engineering, infra and core. This is arguably the highest-leverage open question in the whole design.
facts.short: whether they run their own node (unknown)

facts.statement: We do not know the true maximum object sizes. Parquet footers give averages and per-block averages, not maxima, because Parquet statistics store min/max VALUES rather than value lengths. The largest single source file, metadata blob and per-contract footprint have to come from Sourcify as three MAX(length()) queries.
facts.scope: Only Sourcify can answer. Unit: bytes for max(length(sources.content)), max(length(code.code)), max(length(sourcify_matches.metadata)).

facts.statement: We do not know Sourcify's insert vs update vs delete rates per relation. Their analysis says 75-80% of the database is immutable content-addressed blobs, but sourcify_matches.metadata is updated in place, and there is an open issue about deleting sources from pinning. This decides whether an append-oriented model fits their data at all.
facts.scope: Only Sourcify can answer. Unit: rows inserted / updated / deleted per day per relation.

facts.statement: We do not know how much of the 949.6 GB is indexes rather than rows. We have per-table pg_total_relation_size totals from their export stats but not the split, and measuring it on our own copy would reflect our index choices and none of their history.
facts.scope: Only Sourcify can answer. Unit: pg_table_size and pg_indexes_size per table -- ten rows from one read-only query.

facts.statement: The September POC should be one demo, not two experiments: a Sourcify-compatible endpoint backed by Arkiv, answering real queries about real contracts, with a parity panel comparing our answers to theirs byte for byte, plus a write path showing a new verification landing and becoming queryable. It is built along two axes of evidence -- correctness (100k stratified verification heads plus a 10k subset carried with its full dependency closure) and capacity (one hot read route chosen by Sourcify) -- but those are how it gets built, not two things to show. No production cutover.
facts.scope: OUR PROPOSAL for Monday, not agreed with Sourcify

facts.statement: Proposed gates: 100% hash parity on the lossless subcorpus, idempotent re-import with no duplicates, resume from cursor after a crash, and for the capacity axis a replay at 2x Sourcify's measured peak with latency and error thresholds set by them rather than invented by us. The meeting should end with five named outputs: pilot surface chosen by Sourcify, their data owner, our technical owner, agreed success gates, and a date for the first replay.
facts.scope: OUR PROPOSAL

facts.statement: Contracts are deployed as bytecode, which is unreadable. Verification proves a given source compiles to exactly that bytecode: you submit the sources plus the exact compiler version and settings, Sourcify recompiles, and compares the result against what is actually on chain.
facts.scope: the core operation Sourcify performs

facts.statement: A recompile never matches the chain byte for byte, because some differences are legitimate. Sourcify applies transformations to account for them: constructor arguments appended at deploy time, library addresses linked in, immutable values written at construction, the metadata hash itself, and library call protection. If what remains matches, the contract is verified.
facts.scope: why verified_contracts stores creation/runtime transformations and values

facts.statement: The central idea of the schema: a verified contract is a LINK between something deployed and something compiled. contract_deployments describes what is on chain, compiled_contracts describes a compilation, and verified_contracts joins the two and records the transformations needed to get from one to the other.
facts.scope: the shape any replacement data model has to reproduce

facts.statement: Bytecode and source files are deduplicated across all chains and keyed by hash: ERC20.sol is stored once no matter how many contracts include it. That is why the code and sources tables are far smaller than 43.78M contracts would suggest, and why the join tables exist at all.
facts.scope: already content-addressed by Sourcify today -- the part that maps cleanly onto hash-addressed storage

facts.statement: Sourcify stores far more than source and ABI. Per contract: the source files and the standard JSON input, compiler and every setting, ABI, NatSpec userdoc and devdoc, storage layout and transient storage layout, creation and runtime bytecode both as compiled and as deployed, source maps, link references, immutable references, CBOR auxdata positions, the exact transformations applied, deployment details (chain, address, tx hash, block, deployer), and the function, event and error signatures extracted from the ABI.
facts.scope: the full compilation output, which is why the average contract costs ~25.5 KiB

facts.statement: Data arrives three ways: direct verification requests from developers and tools; the Monitor, which watches selected chains for new deployments, reads the metadata hash out of the bytecode and fetches sources from IPFS; and bulk similarity-import jobs that verify contracts by matching bytecode against already-verified ones.
facts.scope: why organic and bulk write regimes look so different

facts.statement: There are four ways to consume the data: the Parquet bulk export at export.sourcify.dev (S3-compatible, daily, append-only), a BigQuery mirror published through Google Cloud Analytics Hub, the API at sourcify.dev/server for one contract at a time, and the browser UI at repo.sourcify.dev.
facts.scope: any replacement has to serve or replace all four

facts.statement: Sourcify is not isolated. It shares the Verifier Alliance database schema with Blockscout and Routescan, forwards every verification it makes to Blockscout, Routescan and Etherscan, is Foundry's default verifier when no Etherscan key is set, and Hardhat v3 verifies everywhere by default. It also runs the 4byte signature service, having taken over openchain.xyz and merged it with 4byte.directory.
facts.scope: this is why they cannot unilaterally change the schema, and why their write volume is growing

facts.statement: Sourcify is a non-profit. It started inside the Ethereum Foundation and spun out into the Argot Collective in 2025, alongside the Solidity project. It is open source and open data: you can run your own instance, and every verified contract is published daily as a downloadable dataset.
facts.scope: relevant to the ownership question: a public good cannot sit behind one private key

facts.statement: Sourcify runs entirely on Google Cloud: the server and monitor on Cloud Run, Postgres on Cloud SQL in europe-west1, BigQuery fed by Datastream change-data-capture off that database, Parquet on GCS, and IPFS pinning via Filebase. The Datastream dependency is the hidden lock-in: its supported-source list is closed, so moving the database off Cloud SQL breaks their analytics pipeline.
facts.scope: from their own July cost review

facts.statement: Sourcify's organic write load is 0.40 verifications per second, which lands about 4.2 rows per second and 10.2 KiB/s of sustained new data (roughly 904 MB/day).
facts.scope: organic steady state, derived from the measured 34,639/day; bulk imports are a separate regime

facts.statement: During a bulk similarity-import their write rate hits 32 verifications per second, about 334 rows per second -- 80x the organic rate. Any capacity plan has to size for the burst, not the average.
facts.scope: measured from the 2026-07-17 single-day spike of 2,774,661 contracts

facts.statement: Across all Sourcify APIs 15M requests/day is about 174 requests per second on average, of which 4byte alone is roughly 81/s (47%) and everything else about 93/s. At 2.31 database transactions per request that is roughly 401 DB transactions per second.
facts.scope: AVERAGE only -- peak is unknown and is the single most important number we still need from Sourcify

facts.statement: 13.6 TB/month of database egress is about 453 GB/day, 5.2 MB/s sustained, or roughly 42 Mbit/s. Spread over all API requests that averages ~30 KB read out of Postgres per request.
facts.scope: database-to-application egress, not client-facing bandwidth; the per-request figure is a rough average across two differently-scoped numbers

facts.statement: The database grows about 24.7 GiB/month organically, which is only 10.0 KiB/s -- roughly 296 GiB/year at the current rate. Storage growth is not the pressure; read serving is.
facts.scope: organic only; bulk imports add far more in bursts

facts.statement: At $373/month for the production database and ~37.5k verifications/day, Sourcify pays roughly $0.00033 per verification and about $0.39 per GB stored per month. Any proposal has to beat a number that small.
facts.scope: derived from their published production DB cost; the whole Cloud SQL fleet is $1,003/month

facts.statement: The authoritative copy of every blob lives INSIDE Postgres, not in a separate object store. Source text is sources.content, bytecode is code.code, the artifacts and metadata are JSON columns. repo.sourcify.dev is not a file server: it redirects to sourcify.dev/server/repository, which reads out of the database. IPFS via Filebase is a pinning MIRROR of sources, and they have an open issue about not being able to delete from it. The GCS Parquet export is a derived daily snapshot.
facts.scope: verified by following repo.sourcify.dev (307 to the server) and by the v2 API returning source content inline

facts.statement: The v2 API serves blob content inline out of the database. Measured on USDC: the default response is 189 bytes, ?fields=abi is 1.5 KB, ?fields=sources is 11.9 KB, and ?fields=all is 75 KB. On Uniswap V3 Factory ?fields=all returns 4.56 MB in one response. So the queryable head is ~189 bytes and the blob payload behind it can be four thousand times larger.
facts.value: 189 B head vs up to 4.56 MB full
facts.scope: measured 2026-08-19 against their production API
facts.short: 189 B head vs 4.56 MB full response

facts.statement: This explains their egress. 13.6 TB/month leaves the database at roughly 30 KB per request on average, and the head record is only 189 bytes -- so essentially all of that egress is blob payload being read out of Postgres and served. That is why their own review concluded a migration only pays if egress drops ~95%, and why they described the fix as redesigning how contracts are served rather than as a storage-price question.
facts.scope: our inference from two measured figures: their egress and our API response measurements

source.label: derived from Sourcify issue #2866 + API measurements

facts.statement: Where the blobs should go, honestly: NOT Arkiv (nothing in the blob set is ever queried -- it is fetched by hash once you know which contract you want, so putting 95.9% of the bytes behind a query engine buys nothing and inherits every size limit). And NOT left in Postgres either, because that is exactly what makes their database 949.6 GB and their egress 13.6 TB/month. The realistic tier is content-addressed object storage behind a CDN: they already run this pattern for the Parquet export, 242 GiB in cloud storage for about $5/month. IPFS pinning stays as the open, mirrorable copy they already publish, and a decentralized blob layer such as Walrus or Filecoin is the option to evaluate if the goal is that no single provider holds the bytes. Arkiv holds the head with the hash; the hash is what makes any of those interchangeable.
facts.scope: OUR PROPOSAL, not agreed with Sourcify. The choice between plain object storage and a decentralized blob layer is a real decision that has not been made.
facts.short: blobs to content-addressed object storage, not Arkiv
